name: Coatlán Zapotec
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed final stress, coded fixed-dominant) rests on the only and best description of the language: a 644-pp Berkeley reference-grammar dissertation by the principal fieldworker, with a dedicated stress section; the quotation is verbatim at sec. 2.2.3, pp. 81-82 (PDF 98-99), verified in the copy downloaded now. The author's 2018 handout and 2023 JHL article independently restate a single (final) prominent syllable per word. Nothing found suggests a different coding. Two housekeeping points: (a) the record's grade/quote/cite/loc top-level fields are blank although sources[0] carries a verified quotation from an authoritative grammar, so the strength of the evidence should be set/upgraded and loc filled as 'sec. 2.2.3, pp. 81-82'; (b) the 'dominant' (non-strict) flag is defensible only via unreduced compounds ('stress on both roots', p. 84) and syntactic stresslessness (2.2.4); for le

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona 2004, A Coatlan-Loxicha Zapotec Grammar, sec. 2.2.3 (rosemarybeamdeazcona.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/), full section read
sources.quote: Polysyllabic words in CLZ have final stress. ... In sum, an unstressed syllable is any non-final syllable with high tone. All final syllables are stressed and the prominence which is stress can be attained either by a non-high tone or by syllable weight or both.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2023. 'The tonal morphology of the potential in Coatec Zapotec (Di'zhke'): implications for early Zapotecan tone, *ʔ, and verb classes through internal and comparative reconstruction'. Journal of Historical Linguistics (author's last preprint).
sources.quote: 'Every phonological word in Coatec has a single prominent syllable, which bears one of these five tones. Other than loanwords (e.g., /eskoˈpét/ 'shotgun') and compounds (e.g., /jit͡ʃèk/ ...), most words are monosyllabic due to the loss of unstressed vowels'; pre-tonic syllables occur mostly in compounds and loans with tonal contrasts neutralized.
sources.locator: sec. 2 (preprint text around ex. (8)) and sec. 4.1.1
sources.note: Most recent statement by the same author: one prominent syllable per phonological word, final in loans/compounds; independent confirmation 19 years after the grammar.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2018. 'Tono, prosodia, registro y la entonación en el di'zhke' (zapoteco coateco)'. Handout, Seminario de Tonología, UNAM, 19 Sept 2018 (60 slides).
sources.quote: 'Prominencia en la última sílaba de compuestos, contrastes tonales en la sílaba tónica y en los enclíticos únicamente' with example /ŋguzˈndô/ 'ojo'.
sources.note: Prosody-specific handout restating final-syllable prominence in compounds and tonal neutralization in atonic syllables; useful if the domain field (currently not yet coded) is later filled (enclitics bear tone contrasts but are outside the tonic syllable).

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2004. A Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec Grammar. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley.
sources.quote: 'Polysyllabic words in CLZ have final stress.' ... 'All final syllables are stressed'; unstressed (pre-tonic) syllables carry only high tone; reduced compounds and all loanwords have final stress (post-tonic Spanish vowels deleted); unreduced compounds described as having stress on both roots.
sources.locator: sec. 2.2.3 Stress, printed pp. 81-82 (pp. 98-99); compounds p. 84; loans pp. 87-88
sources.note: The deciding source itself was not yet obtained; now downloaded and the quotation verified at pp. 81-82.
